title: Apache Iceberg Concepts: Table Format, Time Travel, Partitioning
summary: Iceberg is an open table format that brings database-like reliability (ACID, time travel, schema evolution) to files in a data lake. This module teaches the concepts analysts actually meet: snapshots and time travel for reproducible analysis, hidden partitioning for fast queries, and schema evolution without rewrites — with hands-on practice through DuckDB's Iceberg support.
objectives: Explain what a table format is and why Iceberg exists (files alone lack transactions, schema evolution, and consistent reads)
Describe snapshots, manifests, and metadata files, and use time travel to query a table as of a past point
Contrast hidden partitioning with traditional directory partitioning and explain the performance difference
Apply schema evolution (add/rename/widen columns) without rewriting existing data
Read and write Iceberg tables from DuckDB to practice the concepts on a laptop

notes.title: The problem Iceberg solves: files are not tables
notes.body:
- A data lake full of Parquet files is cheap storage, but files alone give you no transactions (two writers can corrupt each other), no consistent snapshot reads, and painful schema changes.
- A table format is a metadata layer on top of the files: it tracks which files belong to the table, what the schema is, and the history of changes — so readers always see a consistent view.
- Iceberg's design: a metadata file points to a snapshot; the snapshot points to manifest files; manifests list the actual data files. Every write creates a NEW snapshot — old snapshots stay, which is what makes time travel possible.
- ACID in plain terms: a write either fully lands as a new snapshot or it doesn't — readers never see a half-written table.

```sql
-- DuckDB can read an Iceberg table's metadata: which snapshots exist?
SELECT snapshot_id, committed_at, summary
FROM iceberg_snapshots('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
```

notes.title: Time travel: reproducible analysis without backups
notes.body:
- Because every write is a new immutable snapshot, you can query the table exactly as it looked at any past snapshot or timestamp.
- Analyst use cases: 're-run last quarter's report on the data as it was then' (reproducibility), 'what did this row look like before the backfill?' (debugging), incident forensics.
- Two flavors: by snapshot id (exact) or by timestamp (as-of — resolves to the latest snapshot before that time).
- Discipline: time travel shows you old DATA, not old LOGIC — re-running an old query file against an old snapshot is the full reproducibility story; pair both in version control.

```sql
-- What did the table look like before today's backfill?
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount) AS revenue_then
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg',
                  version => '2026-10-01 00:00:00');

-- Compare then vs now in one query
WITH then_t AS (
  SELECT SUM(amount) AS rev FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg', version => '2026-10-01 00:00:00')
),
now_t AS (
  SELECT SUM(amount) AS rev FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg')
)
SELECT then_t.rev AS revenue_oct1, now_t.rev AS revenue_now,
       now_t.rev - then_t.rev AS delta_from_backfill
FROM then_t, now_t;
```

notes.title: Hidden partitioning: stop thinking about directories
notes.body:
- Traditional Hive-style partitioning bakes the partition into the directory path (year=2026/month=10/...) — queries must know the layout, and changing the partition scheme means rewriting all the data.
- Iceberg's hidden partitioning: you declare a partition transform (e.g. day(order_date), bucket(customer_id, 16)) in the table metadata; the engine maps each row to its partition automatically.
- The analyst benefit: you write `WHERE order_date >= '2026-10-01'` on the plain column — no partition-column gymnastics — and the engine prunes files that can't match.
- Partition evolution: change the partition scheme later (month -> day) and old files keep working — old and new layouts coexist, queries stay the same.

```sql
-- Create an Iceberg table with hidden partitioning via DuckDB
CREATE TABLE orders_iceberg AS
FROM read_csv('orders.csv', header=true);
-- (Conceptually: PARTITIONED BY days(order_date), bucket(customer_id, 16))
-- The analyst query stays clean — pruning happens under the hood:
SELECT region, SUM(amount)
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg')
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-10-01'   -- engine skips non-matching files
GROUP BY region;
```

notes.title: Schema evolution without the rewrite
notes.body:
- In plain Parquet lakes, adding a column means rewriting files or living with inconsistent schemas across partitions.
- Iceberg tracks columns by ID, not position: add a column, rename one, or widen a type (int -> bigint), and old files are read with the new schema — missing values come back as null.
- What you still can't do casually: narrowing types or dropping columns that downstream jobs depend on — evolution is safe, not magic.
- Analyst habit: when a source adds a field mid-quarter, evolve the Iceberg schema forward and document the change date; historical queries keep working because old snapshots keep the old schema view.

```sql
-- Inspect current schema, then evolve it (conceptual DDL)
SELECT field_name, field_type
FROM iceberg_schema('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
-- ALTER TABLE orders_iceberg ADD COLUMN promo_code VARCHAR;
-- Old files: promo_code reads back as NULL. New files: populated.
-- Query across the evolution boundary safely:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_before,
       COUNT(promo_code) AS rows_with_promo
FROM iceberg_scan('warehouse/orders_iceberg');
```

cards.back: A metadata layer over lake files tracking which files belong to the table, the schema, and change history — giving files ACID transactions and consistent reads.
Metadata file -> snapshot -> manifest files -> data files. Each write creates a new snapshot; old snapshots persist.
Query the table as of a past snapshot id or timestamp — reproducible reports and backfill forensics without backups.
Hive bakes partitions into directory paths (queries must know the layout); Iceberg declares transforms in metadata and prunes files automatically from plain WHERE clauses.
Change the partition scheme later (month->day); old files keep working, queries stay unchanged — impossible with directory-based layouts without rewrites.

cards.front: Why Iceberg schema evolution is safe
cards.back: Columns tracked by ID not position: add/rename/widen without rewriting data; old files return null for new columns.
iceberg_scan(path [, version => ...]) for data, iceberg_snapshots(path) for history, iceberg_schema(path) for the schema.
Time travel restores old DATA, not old LOGIC — pair an old snapshot with the version-controlled query file for true reproducibility.

quiz.q: A lake has 10,000 Parquet files and two jobs write at once, corrupting reads. The Iceberg concept that fixes this is:
choices: Atomic snapshots: each write lands as one new immutable snapshot, so readers never see partial writes
Faster Parquet compression
Automatic CSV conversion
Deleting old files nightly
quiz.explain: Snapshot atomicity is the ACID story: all-or-nothing visibility per write. (Module 43)

quiz.q: Last quarter's revenue report must be reproduced exactly on the data as it existed then. You should:
choices: Re-download the source CSVs from email attachments
Query the Iceberg table with time travel at the quarter-end snapshot, using the version-controlled query
Ask the warehouse team to restore from tape
Estimate from the current numbers
quiz.explain: Time travel + versioned query = exact reproduction without restores. (Module 43)

quiz.q: With hidden partitioning on day(order_date), how does an analyst filter to October 2026?
choices: List the October directories manually and UNION them
WHERE partition_day = 'october' using the hidden column directly
WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-10-01' AND order_date < DATE '2026-11-01' — the engine prunes files automatically
It is impossible; hidden partitions cannot be filtered
quiz.explain: Hidden partitioning means plain column predicates; pruning is the engine's job. (Module 43)

quiz.q: The team changes partitioning from month(order_date) to day(order_date). With Iceberg:
choices: All historical data must be rewritten into day directories before any query runs
All queries must be rewritten to reference the new partition columns
Time travel stops working
Old files keep working under the old scheme; new writes use the new scheme; queries are unchanged
quiz.explain: Partition evolution: mixed layouts coexist, query interface stable. (Module 43)

quiz.q: A source adds a promo_code column mid-quarter. Safest Iceberg-native handling:
choices: Rewrite every historical Parquet file to include the column
Create a second table and JOIN forever
Ignore the column until next year
Evolve the schema (ADD COLUMN); old files read promo_code as null; document the change date
quiz.explain: ID-based schema evolution avoids rewrites; nulls for old files is the designed behavior. (Module 43)

quiz.q: Which metadata object lists the actual data files in a snapshot?
choices: The Hive metastore password file
The Parquet footer
The manifest files
The snapshot's nickname
quiz.explain: Chain: metadata file -> snapshot -> manifests -> data files. (Module 43)

quiz.q: An analyst says 'time travel means I can recover any deleted row.' The precise correction:
choices: Time travel is only for schema changes
Time travel lets you query past snapshots, which includes rows as they were — but retention policies may expire old snapshots, so it is not an infinite backup
Time travel only works on CSVs
Deleted rows are unrecoverable by design
quiz.explain: Snapshots persist per retention policy — powerful but not infinite; know the expiry. (Module 43)

quiz.q: Why do analysts practice Iceberg with DuckDB in this course?
choices: DuckDB's Iceberg support lets you read snapshots, schemas, and time-travel locally with zero infrastructure
DuckDB invented Iceberg
Iceberg only runs inside DuckDB
It avoids learning SQL
quiz.explain: Local, zero-infra practice of real concepts — the course's standing approach. (Module 43)

title: dbt Core: Models, Tests, Docs
summary: dbt turns SQL into software engineering: version-controlled models with SELECT statements, automated data tests, and auto-generated documentation. This module covers the model/test/doc/source/fixture workflow end to end using the DuckDB adapter locally — the same patterns that run in production warehouses.
objectives: Structure a dbt project (models, tests, docs, sources) and explain what each layer is for
Write a dbt model as a SELECT with ref() and source() and describe how dbt builds the dependency graph
Add generic and singular data tests (unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values, custom SQL)
Generate and interpret dbt docs (lineage graph, column descriptions, test results)
Run dbt build locally on DuckDB and read the run output to diagnose failures

notes.title: The dbt mental model: SQL with software discipline
notes.body:
- Without dbt: analysts keep 40 SQL files named final_v2_ACTUAL.sql, nobody knows the run order, and 'it worked on my laptop' is the deployment story.
- With dbt: each model is one SELECT statement in a .sql file; dbt compiles them in dependency order, materializes them as tables/views, and versions everything in git.
- `ref('stg_orders')` = 'build the model named stg_orders first, then use it' — dbt draws the DAG from your ref() calls, so run order is derived, never hand-scheduled.
- `source('raw', 'orders')` = 'read the raw table orders from the raw schema' — sources are declared once in YAML, so every model references raw data the same way.

```sql
-- models/marts/orders_daily.sql: a model is just a SELECT
WITH cleaned AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    CAST(order_date AS DATE) AS order_date,
    amount
  FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}   -- dbt resolves the dependency
  WHERE amount >= 0
)
SELECT
  order_date,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM cleaned
GROUP BY order_date
```

notes.title: Project layout: staging, intermediate, marts
notes.body:
- Convention (not law): staging (stg_) = 1:1 with sources, light cleaning, renamed columns; intermediate (int_) = reusable business logic; marts = wide, analytics-ready tables per domain.
- Materializations: view (default, always fresh, slower), table (persisted, rebuilt each run), incremental (append/update new rows — for large tables).
- Choose per model: small dimensions -> table; huge event logs -> incremental; exploratory -> view.
- Every model gets a YAML entry: description + column descriptions — this is what becomes documentation, and 'undocumented model' is a code-review fail.

```yaml
# models/marts/_marts.yml
version: 2
models:
  - name: orders_daily
    description: "One row per day: order counts and revenue, cleaned. Grain: order_date."
    columns:
      - name: order_date
        description: "Calendar date of the order. Primary grain of this mart."
        tests: [not_null]
      - name: revenue
        description: "Sum of order amounts for the day, refunds excluded."
```

```bash
# Run it locally against DuckDB
 dbt build --profiles-dir .   # builds models, runs tests, in DAG order
```

notes.title: Tests: the data contract you run every time
notes.body:
- Generic tests (built in): unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships (foreign-key check). Declared in YAML, run on every build.
- Singular tests: custom SQL files in tests/ that must return ZERO rows — any row returned is a failure. This is where business rules live ('no negative revenue', 'no future order dates').
- Test severity: error (default, blocks) vs warn (logs, continues) — warn for new rules you're calibrating, error once trusted.
- Senior habit: a model without tests is a draft. Tests are how you prove the pipeline, not just the query, is correct.

```yaml
# generic tests live in the model's YAML
columns:
  - name: order_id
    tests: [unique, not_null]
  - name: customer_id
    tests:
      - relationships:
          to: ref('dim_customers')
          field: customer_id
```

```sql
-- tests/no_future_orders.sql: singular test, must return 0 rows
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
WHERE order_date > CURRENT_DATE
```

notes.title: Docs and lineage: dbt docs generate
notes.body:
- `dbt docs generate` + `dbt docs serve` builds a local website: every model, its SQL, its column descriptions, its tests and their status, and the full lineage DAG.
- Lineage answers the stakeholder question 'where does this dashboard number come from?' — click the mart, walk the graph back to raw sources.
- Exposures (declared in YAML) link dashboards to the models that feed them, so a model change shows which dashboards are affected.
- Workflow discipline: dbt build (models+tests) -> dbt docs generate -> review lineage before merging. Docs are a build artifact, not a wiki page you write later.

```yaml
# models/exposures.yml — tie the dashboard to its models
version: 2
exposures:
  - name: executive_revenue_dashboard
    type: dashboard
    owner: {name: analytics-team}
    depends_on:
      - ref('orders_daily')
      - ref('dim_customers')
```

```bash
dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve --port 8080
# open localhost:8080 -> lineage graph, column docs, test results
```

cards.back: One .sql file containing a SELECT; dbt compiles models in dependency order and materializes them as tables/views.
ref('model') = depend on another dbt model (builds the DAG); source('raw','t') = read a declared raw table.
Staging: 1:1 with sources, light cleaning. Intermediate: reusable logic. Marts: wide analytics-ready tables per domain.
view (always fresh), table (rebuilt each run), incremental (append/update new rows for large tables).
Generic: built-ins (unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships) declared in YAML. Singular: custom SQL in tests/ that must return zero rows.
warn logs and continues (calibrating a new rule); error blocks the run (trusted rule).
A local site: model SQL, column descriptions, test results, and the full lineage DAG from sources to marts.
Which dashboards/analyses depend on which models — so a model change shows affected downstream consumers.

quiz.q: A model selects from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}. What does dbt do with this?
choices: Adds stg_orders to the dependency graph and builds it before this model
Copies the raw CSV into the project
Ignores it — refs are comments
Emails the owner of stg_orders
quiz.explain: ref() is how the DAG is derived: dependencies build first, automatically. (Module 44)

quiz.q: Where should the rule 'order amounts must never be negative' live?
choices: In a slide deck
As a singular test: SQL returning any violating rows, which fails the build if non-empty
As a comment in the model
Nowhere — trust the source
quiz.explain: Business rules become singular tests: zero rows = pass, any row = failure. (Module 44)

quiz.q: A 500M-row events table rebuilds from scratch every run and takes hours. Best materialization change?
choices: Switch to a view
Delete the model
Switch to incremental so only new/changed rows are processed
Run it more often
quiz.explain: Incremental materialization processes deltas instead of full rebuilds — the large-table pattern. (Module 44)

quiz.q: The stakeholder asks 'where does the revenue number on the dashboard come from?' Your fastest honest answer uses:
choices: The dbt docs lineage graph: click the mart, trace back through refs to declared sources
The dashboard's color scheme
A guess based on table names
Your memory of writing it
quiz.explain: Lineage is the auditable answer: model -> refs -> sources, all generated from code. (Module 44)

quiz.q: A new data-quality rule is uncalibrated and might fire on legacy quirks. How do you introduce it?
choices: As error immediately on all historical data
Skip tests for legacy data
Delete the legacy data
As severity: warn first — observe failures without blocking, promote to error once trusted
quiz.explain: warn-then-error is the disciplined rollout: calibrate before you block. (Module 44)

quiz.q: What does source('raw', 'orders') give you that a hardcoded schema.table reference does not?
choices: Faster query execution
Automatic data cleaning
A single declared definition of raw inputs, so every model references the same source identically and docs show source freshness/lineage
A backup of the table
quiz.explain: Sources centralize raw-table declarations: consistency + lineage + documentation in one place. (Module 44)

quiz.q: dbt build fails on a relationships test between orders.customer_id and dim_customers. Most likely meaning:
choices: The database is offline
Orphaned foreign keys: orders reference customer_ids missing from dim_customers
dbt is not installed
The YAML has a typo in every case
quiz.explain: relationships = foreign-key check; failure means child rows point at missing parents. (Module 44)

quiz.q: Why does this course run dbt against DuckDB locally instead of starting on a cloud warehouse?
choices: DuckDB adapter runs the identical dbt workflow (models, tests, docs) with zero cloud setup or cost
dbt only supports DuckDB
Cloud warehouses cannot run dbt
It avoids writing SQL
quiz.explain: Same discipline, zero infrastructure: the workflow transfers directly to any warehouse later. (Module 44)
